entries.title: There's a specific 'unforgivable sin' (blasphemy against the Holy Spirit) that you can commit by accident, even with a stray thought or doubt, and once you do, God will never forgive you.
entries.summary: If you're afraid you've committed the unforgivable sin, that fear is itself strong evidence you haven't. Jesus was describing a settled, hardened refusal to call good evil, not a passing thought.
entries.explain:
If you're reading this because you're scared you crossed a line you can't undo, it's worth knowing up front: the fear itself usually points away from the thing Jesus was describing, not toward it. The passage is Mark 3:28-30 (paralleled in Matthew 12:31-32), and the setting matters as much as the wording. Jesus had just cast out a demon in front of religious leaders who had traveled specifically to watch him. Rather than reckon with what they'd witnessed, they announced their verdict on the spot: he does this by the power of Satan, not God. That's the whole context: people who watched God's own power at work, in person, and chose to call it evil.

Blasphemy, in the Greek of the New Testament, is a broad word for attacking someone's honor with speech (slander, defamation), aimed here at the Holy Spirit specifically. What made this particular act unforgivable wasn't a specific sentence someone said, but the posture it revealed: a heart so set against God that it looks directly at His work and names it evil, and keeps doing so. Mark even underlines the target a verse later, explaining that Jesus said this "because they were saying, 'he has an unclean spirit,'" tying the warning to that specific, sustained accusation against His ministry, not to a general list of forbidden words or thoughts.

This is one of the most quietly damaging fears in ordinary Christian life, and one of the most consistent things pastors and counselors report is also the simplest: people who are anxious they've committed this sin have not committed it. The sin described is a comfortable, hardened rejection of God, not a troubled conscience wondering if a stray doubt went too far. A conscience that's unsettled by the question is doing exactly what the Holy Spirit does: convicting, not condemning. The warning in Mark 3 was for people confidently calling God's work evil while they watched it happen in front of them. It was never aimed at someone lying awake wondering if they'd lost their footing with God; wondering that is, itself, proof you haven't.

entries.title: 'The Rapture' is a biblical term: Scripture itself uses the word 'rapture' for believers being caught up to meet Jesus.
entries.summary: The word 'rapture' never appears in any English Bible translation. It comes from the Latin Vulgate's rendering of 1 Thessalonians 4:17, and the specific end-times doctrine built on it is about two centuries old.
entries.explain:
1 Thessalonians 4:17 is real, and it does describe believers being "caught up" together with the Lord in the clouds. The Greek verb there is harpazo (ἁρπάζω), "to snatch" or "seize." When Jerome translated the New Testament into Latin for the Vulgate around 400 AD, he rendered that verb as rapiemur, from the Latin rapio, "to seize" or "carry off," the same root behind English words like "rapacious" and "rapture." English Bible translations, though, render the Greek directly as "caught up," not "raptured." So "rapture" isn't a translation choice at all. It's a theological label that entered English through a Latin gloss on the passage, not through any English Bible text. Harpazo itself is ordinary New Testament vocabulary: it is the verb for Philip being carried off by the Spirit at Acts 8:39, and Paul uses it of being caught up into the third heaven at 2 Corinthians 12:2.

The label is old and traceable; the specific doctrine now attached to it (a "Rapture" as a distinct, pre-tribulation removal of the church from earth ahead of a period of end-times judgment, followed later by Christ's visible return) is much younger than the word. That systematized version traces to John Nelson Darby (1800-1882), the Anglo-Irish founder of the Plymouth Brethren, who wrote in 1850 that he'd arrived at the framework around 1830. It reached a mass American audience through the Scofield Reference Bible, published in 1909, which built Darby's dispensational timeline directly into its widely-read study notes.

None of this means 1 Thessalonians 4:17 describes nothing, or that pretribulationism was invented out of thin air. It's a real reading of real texts, held by serious people, and disagreeing about timing doesn't make it dishonest. What's fair to say plainly: the word "rapture" is a sixteen-hundred-year-old Latin label attached to a Greek verb, and the fully worked-out doctrine of a separate, pre-tribulation "Rapture event" is a nineteenth-century systemization, not a term the apostles used, and not a timeline the earliest church held. The event language is biblical. The word is Latin. The specific timing scheme is about two hundred years old.

entries.title: The Bible teaches a threefold demonology: 'unclean spirits,' 'familiar spirits,' and 'seducing spirits' are three distinct categories of evil spirit, each requiring different handling.
entries.summary: All three phrases are genuinely biblical, but they're three unrelated words from three different parts of Scripture; nobody in the Bible ever lines them up into a single taxonomy.
entries.explain:
"Unclean spirit" (Greek pneuma akatharton) is Gospel-and-Acts vocabulary, showing up in exorcism accounts across Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts, with a single similar phrase back in Zechariah 13:2. The Gospel writers themselves use "unclean spirit," "evil spirit," and "demon" interchangeably within the same stories: Mark will call the same being an unclean spirit in one verse and a demon in the next. That alone shows it isn't marking off a special category; it's one of several overlapping ways the Gospels describe the affliction Jesus casts out.

"Familiar spirit" is something else entirely. It's the King James rendering of the Hebrew ob, an Old Testament term tied to necromancy, most famously the medium of Endor whom Saul consulted in 1 Samuel 28. "Familiar" here doesn't mean "well-known," the way it sounds to modern ears. The translators (following the earlier Geneva Bible) borrowed the Latin familiaris, a household servant or intimate of the family, to describe a spirit supposedly bound to a medium the way an attendant is bound to a household. It's a sixteenth-century English word doing a job that sense of the word no longer does in modern English.

"Seducing spirits" appears exactly once, in 1 Timothy 4:1, and the underlying Greek word (planos) doesn't carry a romantic sense of seduction at all; it means "wandering" or "leading astray," the same image used elsewhere for a lost sheep. Paul is warning about false teaching and doctrinal apostasy in the last days, not describing an exorcism or a necromancy ritual. Set the three side by side and they don't touch: one is Gospel exorcism language, one is Old Testament necromancy language carrying a centuries-old English translation choice, and one is Pauline language about false teachers. Every word is genuinely in the Bible. The "three types of spirits" system that treats them as one unified taxonomy (implying three different categories each needing its own deliverance method) is something readers built on top of three separate words that were never meant to sit on the same shelf.

entries.title: John the Baptist wasn't really eating bugs: the 'locusts' in the Gospels were actually carob pods
entries.summary: The Greek word is akris, the standard term for the insect, and the carob idea has no manuscript support at all.
entries.explain:
Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6 both say John's food was akris (ἀκρίς) and wild honey. Akris is the ordinary Greek word for a locust, the same word used for the locust plagues in Revelation, and it's exactly the food Leviticus 11:22 lists as one of the few insects Jews were allowed to eat. There's no textual variant, no alternate manuscript reading, nothing in the Greek that points to a bean pod instead of a bug. Locusts, dried, roasted, or salted, were ordinary desert food for John's era; ancient and modern accounts of Bedouin diet both mention them.

The carob theory rides on a coincidence of naming, not a translation problem. Carob pods are nicknamed 'St. John's bread' and were sometimes called 'locust bean' or 'locust pods' in English and other languages because the pods vaguely resemble a locust's curved body: the insect gave its name to the plant, not the other way around. Separately, the Gospel of the Ebionites, a lost second-century text known mainly through quotations by church fathers, changed John's diet to honey cakes, apparently because the Ebionites practiced vegetarianism and were uncomfortable with an ascetic prophet eating meat (some manuscripts of that gospel swap akrides, locusts, for enkrides, cakes, a one-letter pun in Greek). That's a theologically motivated edit in a fringe text, not a discovery about what Matthew and Mark actually wrote.

So this is a myth that runs backwards from most entries on this list: the plain, traditional reading (John ate actual locusts) is the one the Greek and the historical record support. The 'actually carob' version is the popular-sounding revision, and it's the one without a textual leg to stand on.

entries.title: Satan was heaven's worship leader, built with tabrets and pipes, which is why he attacks music
entries.summary: Modern translations render those Hebrew words as jeweled settings, not musical instruments, and the oracle is addressed to the king of Tyre.
entries.explain:
The whole worship-leader legend hangs on one clause in the KJV of Ezekiel 28:13: 'the workmanship of thy tabrets and of thy pipes was prepared in thee.' The Hebrew word behind 'pipes' there, neqev, appears exactly once in the entire Old Testament, which makes it genuinely hard to translate. The KJV translators connected it to a root about piercing and guessed at percussion and wind instruments. But the rest of the verse is a list of nine gemstones (ruby, topaz, diamond, beryl, and so on), so most modern translations read neqev the same way: as jeweler's language, not musician's. The NIV has 'your settings and mountings were made of gold,' the ESV has 'your settings and your engravings,' and the NASB and the LSB both read 'the workmanship of your settings and sockets.' None of them say 'pipes' or 'tabrets.'

It's also worth being honest that scholars don't fully agree on everything in this passage: the Eden imagery in Ezekiel 28 draws on ideas and language that show up elsewhere in ancient Near Eastern literature, and there's real debate about how much of verses 12-19 describes the human king of Tyre alone versus gesturing at a supernatural figure behind him (the 'anointed cherub who covers' in verse 14 is part of that debate). What isn't disputed is the addressee: verse 12 says explicitly, 'take up a lamentation over the king of Tyre.' Whatever else is going on in the passage, it's a funeral dirge for a human ruler's pride and fall, dressed in the most exalted imagery the prophet had. Nothing in the Hebrew text assigns Satan a musical office, and the entire warfare-against-worship theology built on top of it is downstream of one English phrase from 1611.
entries.tags: satan ezekiel-28 worship music hebrew tyre

entries.title: The Second Law of Thermodynamics proves evolution is scientifically impossible because entropy only increases
entries.summary: The second law governs closed systems, and Earth isn't one: it runs on a continuous stream of energy from the sun.
entries.explain:
The second law of thermodynamics does say that the total entropy of an isolated system never decreases over time. The argument leaves out the word 'isolated.' An isolated system is one that exchanges neither matter nor energy with anything outside it: a sealed, insulated box. Earth is not that. It's an open system, constantly bathed in energy from the sun and constantly radiating heat back out into space. Local pockets of that system can become more ordered (a seed growing into a plant, a fertilized egg developing into an embryo, water freezing into a snowflake's crystal structure) without breaking any law, because the ordering is paid for by energy flowing through the system and entropy being exported elsewhere. None of that is controversial physics; it's the same reason a refrigerator can get colder inside while the room around it gets warmer.

What's notable is that this isn't just secular scientists correcting an outside argument: plenty of Christian organizations that hold a young-earth or design-friendly position, including ones that reject evolution on other grounds, have publicly said this specific argument doesn't work and shouldn't be used, because any physicist can dismantle it in one sentence. That matters more than it might seem: an argument that gets a strong believer laughed out of a room doesn't just fail on its own, it makes every other argument on the same platform sound less credible by association.

A quick note on fit for this tool: this isn't a Bible-verse claim at all, it's a piece of pop-apologetics reasoning that circulates in Christian culture, so there's no scripture reference to correct it against. It's included here because it behaves exactly like the other entries: a claim that sounds authoritative, gets repeated confidently, and turns out not to hold up under a plain reading of the source material, in this case a physics textbook instead of a Bible passage.

entries.title: The church building is the house of God, which is why you have to be reverent and quiet inside it
entries.summary: The New Testament applies temple language to believers themselves, not to church architecture.
entries.explain:
The Greek word naos refers specifically to the inner sanctuary of a temple: the actual dwelling place of a deity, as distinct from hieron, the wider temple complex and courts. Paul uses naos three times to describe people, not buildings. To the church at Corinth he writes that 'you are a sanctuary of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you'; naos is the word translated 'sanctuary' there (1 Corinthians 3:16, and he says the same of the individual body in 1 Corinthians 6:19). In Ephesians 2:19-22, believers are 'no longer strangers... but... of God's household,' and 'the whole building, being joined together, is growing into a holy sanctuary in the Lord'; naos again, present tense, still under construction, made of people being joined to each other. Peter uses a related image without the word naos itself: believers are 'living stones... built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood' (1 Peter 2:5). Three different New Testament writers, three passages, all landing on the same move: temple language gets pulled off the architecture and put onto the gathered and individual believer.

That's a real theological point, and it's worth being fair to the instinct it's correcting rather than steamrolling it. Sacred space is a genuine biblical category: Eden, the tabernacle, Solomon's temple, and the final vision of a city with no temple at all because 'the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its sanctuary' (Revelation 21:22) all treat the presence of God as something that sanctifies a place. The New Testament isn't saying that category was a mistake. It's saying the category moved: God's dwelling now sits in his people rather than in a building, so the reverence instinct people have walking into a church isn't wrong, it's just aimed at the wrong address. A church building can still be useful, dedicated, and set apart for gathering; that's a real thing a congregation can choose to do with a space. It's just not what the Bible calls 'the house of God' in the way the phrase usually gets used.

entries.title: There's a real, historically accurate face of Jesus: the one you picture is what he actually looked like
entries.summary: None of the four Gospels describe what Jesus looked like: every familiar face was supplied later, by art, not by scripture.
entries.explain:
Search the Gospels for a description of Jesus's height, build, hair, eyes, or skin, and you'll find nothing. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, writing from either firsthand memory or eyewitness testimony, never once tell you what he looked like. Some scholars, including historian Joan Taylor, have argued the silence itself is a data point: if Jesus had stood out physically, someone would likely have said so, and its absence suggests he looked like an ordinary Galilean Jewish man of his time. One detail in the arrest narrative points the same direction: Judas has to identify Jesus with a kiss in the dark, which only makes sense if he didn't stand out from the other men around him.

Every specific face that has since become 'the' face of Jesus was filled in by later culture. The clearest case is Warner Sallman's 1940 painting Head of Christ, which by the publishers' own count and multiple historians' estimates has been reproduced more than 500 million times, making it a serious contender for the most reproduced image of a religious figure in history. It became the default mental picture of Jesus in American homes, churches, and Sunday school rooms for generations, and for many people it feels like memory rather than a mid-twentieth-century artist's specific choices about hair, eye color, and expression. The pattern repeats: Jim Caviezel's 2004 portrayal in The Passion of the Christ and Jonathan Roumie's ongoing portrayal in The Chosen have each become the current generation's mental default the same way Sallman's painting did for an earlier one.

None of this is an argument against depicting Jesus at all: that's a separate and serious theological conversation. Orthodox and Catholic icon tradition, defended historically by figures like John of Damascus during the iconoclast controversy, argues that because God actually took on a visible human body in the incarnation, depicting Christ is theologically appropriate in a way that depicting the invisible Father isn't. That's a live, considered position, not a mistake to be corrected. The narrower point stands regardless: whatever face comes to mind when you picture Jesus, whether a painting, an actor, or an icon, the Bible didn't put it there. Culture did.

entries.title: "To you it shall be for meat" means God is handing Adam and Eve literal cuts of animal flesh to eat
entries.summary: In 1611 English, "meat" just meant food in general, not animal flesh specifically.
entries.explain:
Genesis 1:29 has God giving Adam "every herb bearing seed... and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat." That's a vegetarian diet being called "meat." The word came from Old English "mete," which simply meant food or nourishment of any kind: the sense survives in fossil phrases like "sweetmeat" (a candy) and "meat and drink to me." Matthew 3:4 does the same thing describing John the Baptist's "meat" as locusts and wild honey.

The narrower modern sense (meat as specifically animal flesh) split off later and gradually took over the word, so a reader who doesn't know the shift pictures God authorizing carnivory in Eden, which is the opposite of the point being made.

entries.title: "They spoiled the Egyptians" means the Israelites vandalized or ruined the Egyptians on their way out
entries.summary: "Spoiled" here means plundered or stripped of goods, not ruined or damaged.
entries.explain:
Exodus 12:36 reads, "the LORD gave the people favour in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they lent unto them such things as they required. And they spoiled the Egyptians." "Spoil" comes from Latin "spoliare," to strip or plunder, the same root that gives us "the spoils of war." The Israelites walked out with the Egyptians' silver, gold, and clothing; that's the "spoiling."

Today "spoil" almost always means to ruin something (spoiled milk, a spoiled child), a sense that developed later and now dominates the word. A modern reader pictures property damage; the text describes a peaceful, almost comic handover of valuables.

entries.title: "Let judgment run down as waters" means let condemnation and punishment pour down on sinners
entries.summary: "Judgment" here means justice, fair and right dealing, not condemnation.
entries.explain:
Amos 5:24 pairs "judgment" directly with "righteousness": "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." That parallel is the tell: Amos wants abundant, unstoppable justice in Israel's courts and streets, not abundant condemnation. "Judgment" in this older, broader sense means the fair administration of a case, the same sense preserved in "the judgment of Solomon" or a courtroom "judgment."

Modern English has narrowed "judgment" toward its negative pole: "don't judge me," "the judgment of God" as a synonym for wrath, so a reader who only knows that sense misses that Amos is demanding more fairness, not more doom.

entries.title: "Provide things honest in the sight of all men" just means don't lie to people
entries.summary: "Honest" meant honorable or respectable in general conduct, not merely truth-telling.
entries.explain:
Romans 12:17 says, "Recompense to no man evil for evil. Provide things honest in the sight of all men." Paul isn't just telling Christians to avoid lying; he's telling them to conduct themselves in a way that looks honorable and above reproach to outside observers. "Honest" in 1611 English covered the whole territory now split between "honest" (truthful) and "honorable" (respectable, decent, of good repute).

Because modern "honest" has narrowed almost entirely to truthfulness, a reader can miss that Paul is talking about visible public conduct, reputation and behavior, not just avoiding falsehood.

entries.title: "Corn" throughout the Old Testament refers to maize, the same corn on the cob eaten today
entries.summary: "Corn" meant grain in general (wheat, barley, etc.); maize didn't exist in the biblical Near East.
entries.explain:
Ruth 2:14 has Boaz handing Ruth "parched corn" to eat in the barley fields near Bethlehem; there was no maize anywhere near Iron Age Israel. "Corn" in British English (the KJV translators were English) is simply the generic word for the dominant local grain, the way Americans still say "corn" for maize specifically because that became their dominant grain. It shows up over a hundred times in the KJV, almost always referring to wheat or barley.

American readers in particular default to "corn" meaning maize, since that's the only sense the word carries in American English today, a meaning maize-growing America gave the word centuries after 1611.

entries.title: "The voice of the turtle is heard in our land" means turtles (the shelled reptile) can be heard in springtime
entries.summary: "Turtle" here is short for turtledove, a bird, not the reptile.
entries.explain:
Song of Solomon 2:12 celebrates spring: "the time of the singing of birds is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land." That only makes sense as a bird: turtles (reptiles) don't have a "voice" anyone notices, but turtledoves have a distinctive cooing call that returns with the season as a migratory bird. "Turtle" here comes from Latin "turtur," an imitation of that cooing sound, and has nothing to do with shells.

The reptile sense of "turtle" was still fairly new in English when the KJV was translated in 1611, so in that era "turtle" alone, unqualified, defaulted to the bird. Modern readers have it backwards, since the reptile sense has now completely taken over the plain word "turtle."

entries.title: "An help meet for him" means God made Eve to simply meet or encounter Adam
entries.summary: "Meet" here is an adjective meaning "suitable" or "fitting"; it's two separate words, not one noun.
entries.explain:
Genesis 2:18 reads, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." "Meet" is doing the same job it does in "meet and right" or "it is meet that we thank him"; it's an old adjective for "fitting, suitable, appropriate." So the phrase literally reads "a help (helper) suitable for him," describing Eve's fitness as a companion, not a verb about meeting someone.

Because English later stopped using "meet" as an adjective, readers now instinctively read "help meet" as a single compound noun, and many editions even print it as one word, "helpmeet" or "helpmate," obscuring that the original is a description of suitability, not a job title.
entries.tags: helpmeet meet suitable genesis archaic kjv

entries.title: "Bowels of mercies" is Scripture making a crude joke about intestines
entries.summary: "Bowels" meant the seat of deep emotion and compassion, what we'd now call the heart or gut feeling.
entries.explain:
Colossians 3:12 instructs believers to "put on... bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." In the physiology of the ancient world, strong emotion, especially compassion, was felt in the internal organs, not the heart, so "bowels" was the natural word for deep, gut-level tenderness. It's the same idea behind our own phrase "gut feeling," which is really the last surviving trace of this older way of talking.

Modern English kept "bowels" only in its clinical, digestive sense, so the verse now reads as unintentionally comic or gross to readers who don't know it's simply asking Christians to be deeply, viscerally compassionate.

entries.title: "Ye allow the deeds of your fathers" means the religious leaders merely tolerated or permitted what their fathers did
entries.summary: "Allow" meant approve of or endorse, much stronger than today's sense of "permit."
entries.explain:
In Luke 11:48, Jesus tells the lawyers, "ye bear witness that ye allow the deeds of your fathers: for they indeed killed them, and ye build their sepulchres." This isn't a mild accusation of looking the other way; Jesus is charging them with actively endorsing and approving the murder of the prophets, evidenced by the monuments they build. Root Latin senses behind "allow" carried ideas of praising and crediting, giving it a much stronger, approving force in 1611 English than "permit" does today.

Modern "allow" has weakened to mean simple permission, letting something happen without necessarily agreeing with it, so readers can miss that this is one of the sharper accusations in the passage, not a soft one.

entries.title: "Apt to teach" describes someone who is prone or inclined to lecture people
entries.summary: "Apt" meant fit, skilled, or qualified, not merely "prone to."
entries.explain:
1 Timothy 3:2 lists "apt to teach" among the qualifications for an overseer, from the Greek "didaktikos," meaning skillful in teaching. "Apt" comes from Latin "aptus," fitted or suitable, the same root behind "adapt" and "aptitude." So the phrase is a qualification of competence: this person is equipped and able to teach well.

Modern English mostly uses "apt" in the sense of "likely" or "prone to" ("apt to forget," "apt to fail"), which flips the meaning from a positive skill into a mere tendency, as if Paul just meant someone who talks a lot, rather than someone actually qualified to instruct.

entries.title: "Set a man at variance against his father" means causing a minor disagreement or difference of opinion
entries.summary: "Variance" meant active conflict or division, far stronger than a mild disagreement.
entries.explain:
Matthew 10:35 has Jesus warning, "I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law." The underlying Greek verb means to split or divide in two; this is about families being torn apart over faith, not a friendly difference of opinion at the dinner table.

Today "variance" is a mild, almost technical word (a zoning variance, "some variance in the data"), so a modern reader tends to underread the intensity of what Jesus is actually predicting: real relational rupture, not a minor spat.

entries.title: "Emulations" listed among the works of the flesh means admiring someone and trying to live up to their good example
entries.summary: "Emulations" translates a Greek word for jealousy or rivalry, a vice, not admiration.
entries.explain:
Galatians 5:20 lists "emulations" right alongside "hatred, variance... wrath, strife" as a work of the flesh. The underlying Greek word is "zelos," which can mean either good zeal or, in a bad sense, jealousy and envious rivalry, and Paul clearly means the bad sense here, grouped with obviously destructive sins.

Modern English "emulation" is almost always positive, copying someone worth imitating, striving to match their excellence, so on a first read it looks strange sitting in a list of vices. Once you know it's translating "jealousy," the verse makes sense again.

entries.title: "Seditions" listed among the works of the flesh means specifically plotting armed rebellion against the government
entries.summary: "Seditions" meant factious divisions in any group, not political revolt against a government.
entries.explain:
In Galatians 5:20, "seditions" sits between "strife" and "heresies" in Paul's list of works of the flesh, a list about relational and church sins, not politics. The Greek word behind it (dichostasiai) just means "standings-apart," i.e., factions and divisions, whether in a family, a church, or a community.

Modern English has narrowed "sedition" almost entirely to a legal, political sense, incitement against a government, the kind of thing prosecuted under a Sedition Act, so a reader assumes Paul is condemning political rebels, when he's really condemning people who split up any group they're part of.

entries.title: "Heresies" listed among the works of the flesh means holding incorrect theological beliefs
entries.summary: "Heresies" meant forming a faction or sect through stubborn self-will: the sin is the division, not the doctrine.
entries.explain:
Galatians 5:20's "heresies" translates the Greek "hairesis," literally "a choosing," which came to mean a party, sect, or faction. Paul's complaint is about people who split the church by insisting on their own opinion and gathering followers around it. What's condemned is the wrongness of the resulting divide, not necessarily the truth or falsehood of the belief itself.

Today "heresy" means almost exclusively false doctrine, full stop, with no necessary connection to factionalism. That shift happened later, once church history made "heretical groups" and "doctrinally wrong groups" nearly synonymous, but the KJV word itself is naming the divisiveness.

entries.title: "Let the earth bring forth... cattle" means cows and bulls specifically
entries.summary: "Cattle" meant livestock or domesticated animals generally, not just bovines.
entries.explain:
Genesis 1:24-25 groups "cattle" together with "creeping thing" and "beast of the earth" as categories of land animals: "cattle" there covers tame, domesticated animals broadly (sheep, goats, camels, oxen, donkeys), not specifically cows. The word comes through Old French "chatel" and Latin "capitale," meaning property or capital; livestock was, quite literally, a family's movable wealth, which is also why "cattle" and "chattel" and "capital" are all the same word underneath.

English later narrowed "cattle" down to bovines exclusively, so modern readers picture herds of cows in a text that's actually describing domesticated animals as a whole category.

entries.title: "God commendeth his love toward us" means God speaks well of, or compliments, his own love
entries.summary: "Commendeth" means demonstrates or proves, not praises or compliments.
entries.explain:
Romans 5:8 says, "God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." The verse is describing an action, the cross itself as proof, not God talking about himself. "Commend" here carries its older sense of "put on display, give proof of," from Latin "commendare," to entrust or commit something to demonstrate its worth.

Modern "commend" almost always means to praise or speak favorably of someone ("I commend you for your effort"), which would make the verse sound like God is congratulating himself, rather than backing up a claim about his love with concrete action.

entries.title: "We are of all men most miserable" means Christians are the gloomiest, unhappiest people around
entries.summary: "Miserable" meant pitiable, deserving of pity, not simply unhappy.
entries.explain:
1 Corinthians 15:19 reads, "If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable." Paul's argument is that if there's no resurrection, then Christians who've given up worldly advantage for a false hope are the most pitiable people alive, not that they walk around feeling sad. "Miserable" here comes straight from Latin "miserabilis," "to be pitied," the same root as "misery" and "commiserate."

Modern English kept the subjective, feelings-based sense of "miserable" (personally unhappy) and largely dropped the older, more objective sense (an outside observer's judgment that you're to be pitied), so readers assume Paul is describing an emotional state rather than a status.

entries.title: "Foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient" means crude jokes that are simply badly timed or inconvenient
entries.summary: "Convenient" meant fitting or proper, a moral judgment, not a scheduling one.
entries.explain:
Ephesians 5:4 warns against "filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient." Paul isn't saying crude jokes happen at a bad time; he's saying they're not fitting or appropriate for someone who follows Christ. "Convenient" comes from Latin "convenire," to come together or agree, and in 1611 English still carried that broad sense of "suitable" or "proper."

The modern, narrower sense (handy, easy, well-timed) developed later and now dominates the word, so a reader can miss that this is a statement about moral fittingness, not logistics.

entries.title: "Let us wait on our ministering" means sit around waiting for your turn to serve
entries.summary: "Wait on" meant actively attend to and serve, the opposite of passively waiting.
entries.explain:
Romans 12:7 instructs, "Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering," meaning: whoever has the gift of practical service should throw themselves diligently into that service. "Wait" originally carried the sense of "watch, attend, be on duty"; a "waiter" in a restaurant still literally does this, actively attending to your table rather than passively standing by.

Modern English has drifted "wait" toward meaning idle delay ("wait for the bus"), so on its own the phrase can sound like Paul is telling people to hold off on serving, when he means the exact opposite: get busy serving.

entries.title: "Remove not the ancient landmark" means don't steal or take away the boundary marker your fathers set
entries.summary: "Remove" meant move or shift its position, not take it away entirely.
entries.explain:
Proverbs 22:28 warns, "Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set." The concern isn't someone stealing a boundary stone outright; it's someone quietly nudging it a few feet to encroach on a neighbor's field, an ancient form of property fraud. "Remove" comes from Latin "removere," literally "move back" or "move away," a fairly neutral verb about changing a thing's location.

Modern colloquial English has pushed "remove" toward meaning "take away and eliminate entirely" ("remove the stain," "remove him from office"), which changes the crime being described from quietly shifting a marker to outright theft of it.

entries.title: "The way of the Lord is not equal" means God doesn't treat everyone in exactly the same, identical way
entries.summary: "Equal" meant fair or just, not "the same in every case."
entries.explain:
Ezekiel 18:25 has the people complaining, "The way of the Lord is not equal," to which God responds, "Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal?" This is a debate about fairness and justice in how God judges people based on their own choices, not a debate about mathematical sameness. "Equal," from Latin "aequalis," carried this moral sense of "just, right" alongside its quantitative sense.

Modern English has let the quantitative sense ("equal amounts," "equal parts") crowd out the older qualitative one, so readers picture a complaint about inconsistency rather than what's actually being argued: whether God's justice is fair.

entries.title: "Incontinent" listed among the vices of the last days refers to a lack of bladder control
entries.summary: "Incontinent" meant lacking self-control generally, especially over fleshly appetites.
entries.explain:
2 Timothy 3:3 lists "incontinent" among traits of people in the last days: "Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good." This is a moral vice list, and "incontinent" here means someone who can't restrain their appetites or passions, from Latin "continere," to hold together or restrain. "Continent" once simply meant self-controlled in general.

In the twentieth century, "incontinent" narrowed almost entirely to a medical term for loss of bladder or bowel control, so a modern reader can badly misjudge what Paul is actually condemning: unrestrained, undisciplined living, not a physical condition.

entries.title: "Enlargement and deliverance shall arise to the Jews" means the Jewish people's territory will get bigger
entries.summary: "Enlargement" meant relief or freedom from confinement, not a bigger territory or size.
entries.explain:
In Esther 4:14, Mordecai tells Esther that if she stays silent, "then shall there enlargement and deliverance arise to the Jews from another place." "Enlargement" and "deliverance" are functioning as near-synonyms here, both about the Jews being rescued and set free from the threat of annihilation, not about acquiring more land. "Enlarge" comes from Latin "largus," abundant or generous, and originally meant to release someone from confinement; the phrase "at large," meaning free rather than imprisoned, preserves that older sense.

Modern English uses "enlarge" almost exclusively to mean "make bigger" (enlarge a photo, enlarge a house), which misses that Mordecai is talking about liberation from danger, not expansion.

entries.title: "Be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess" just means don't drink more than a moderate amount
entries.summary: "Excess" here names a whole lifestyle of reckless, dissolute living, not merely too large a quantity.
entries.explain:
Ephesians 5:18 warns, "be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess." The underlying Greek word ("asotia") describes a life abandoned to sensuality, wasteful indulgence, and moral riot, the kind of drunken revelry associated with pagan festivals in the ancient world, not simply drinking one glass too many. "Excess" comes from Latin "excedere," to go beyond or exceed, and in this context carries that stronger classical force.

Modern English uses "excess" as a fairly mild, almost neutral word for "too much of something" (excess baggage, excess weight), so a reader can badly undersell what Paul is actually warning against: a whole dissolute way of life, not just overindulgence at a party.

entries.title: "Lest your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting" means being charged too much money for your indulgences
entries.summary: "Overcharged" meant weighed down or burdened, nothing to do with price.
entries.explain:
Luke 21:34 warns, "take heed to yourselves, lest at any time your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting, and drunkenness, and cares of this life." "Charge" here comes from the same root as "cargo" and a cart's "load" (Latin "carricare," to load); to be "overcharged" is to be overloaded or weighed down, in this case by excess and worry, so that spiritual alertness gets crushed under the load.

The financial sense of "charge" (billing someone money) is a later specialization of the same "load" idea (you're "charged" a cost) that has now become the dominant meaning of the word, leaving modern readers picturing an unfair bill rather than a burdened, weighed-down heart.

entries.title: "Ye did communicate with my affliction" means the Philippians talked to Paul about his suffering
entries.summary: "Communicate" meant to share or give materially, not to exchange words.
entries.explain:
Philippians 4:14 says, "ye have well done, that ye did communicate with my affliction." Paul is thanking the Philippians for the practical, material support (money and supplies) they sent him during his hardship, not for a conversation. "Communicate" comes from Latin "communicare," to make common or share, the same root behind "community" and "common."

Modern English narrowed "communicate" almost entirely to the exchange of information or messages, so a reader today pictures letters or check-ins rather than what actually happened: the Philippian church sharing their resources to bear Paul's burden with him.

entries.title: "They fetched a compass" means the sailors used a navigational compass instrument to find their way
entries.summary: "Fetched a compass" meant made a circuit or sailed a curving loop, no instrument involved.
entries.explain:
Acts 28:13 describes Paul's sea voyage: "from thence we fetched a compass, and came to Rhegium." This is a now-obsolete idiom for tracing a circular or roundabout course, from the same root as the drawing tool called a "compass" (from Latin/Old French "compassare," to pace out or go around); the emphasis is on the circling motion, not a magnetized needle-and-dial device used for navigation.

Today "compass" almost exclusively means the navigational instrument, so modern readers naturally but wrongly picture the crew consulting a compass, when the verse is simply saying the ship sailed a curving, roundabout route along the coast.

entries.title: "By good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple" means honest, straightforward talk wins over simple people
entries.summary: "Fair speeches" meant smooth, flattering talk designed to manipulate, the opposite of honest.
entries.explain:
Romans 16:18 warns about false teachers who "by good words and fair speeches deceive the hearts of the simple." "Fair" here doesn't mean fair as in just or impartial; it means pleasing, smooth, attractive to the ear, the same sense behind "fair-weather" or a poetic "fair maiden." The whole point of the verse is that this kind of talk sounds good precisely so it can deceive.

Modern English mostly uses "fair" to mean just or evenhanded ("that's not fair"), so a reader can flip the verse's meaning entirely, imagining Paul is warning against straightforward, equitable speech, when he's actually warning against flattering, deceptive smooth-talk.

entries.title: "Patience worketh experience" means going through hard times just gives you more life experience and stories to tell
entries.summary: "Experience" translates a Greek word for proven, tested character, not accumulated life events.
entries.explain:
Romans 5:4 traces a chain: "patience, experience; and experience, hope." The Greek word behind "experience" is "dokime," meaning the proven quality something has after passing a test, closer to "approvedness" or "tested character" than to having lived through a lot. Paul's argument is that endurance under trial produces a tested, proven character, which in turn produces hope, not that suffering simply broadens your resume of experiences.

"Experience" comes from Latin "experiri," to try or test (the same root as "experiment" and "expert"), which is exactly the sense Paul means. Modern English uses "experience" almost entirely for "things you've lived through," flattening Paul's actual point about tested, approved character.

entries.title: "Let your moderation be known unto all men" means be careful to eat, drink, and spend in moderation
entries.summary: "Moderation" meant gentleness and reasonableness toward others, not dietary or financial restraint.
entries.explain:
Philippians 4:5 says, "Let your moderation be known unto all men. The Lord is at hand." Paul is talking about a relational quality (gentleness, forbearance, a willingness to give up your strict rights rather than insist on them), not about avoiding overindulgence in food or spending. Commentators describe it as "sweet reasonableness," a yielding, gracious posture toward other people.

Modern "moderation" is almost entirely about quantity (moderation in eating, drinking, screen time), so a reader misses that Paul is describing a way of treating people, not a rule about self-restraint in consumption.

entries.title: "In watchings often" means Paul spent a lot of time watching or observing things
entries.summary: "Watchings" meant sleepless nights, staying awake through toil or danger, not observing something.
entries.explain:
2 Corinthians 11:27 lists Paul's hardships: "In weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness." "Watchings" belongs with the other physical hardships in that list: it means loss of sleep, staying up because of labor, danger, prayer, or travel, essentially what we'd now call sleepless nights or vigils.

Modern English uses "watch" mainly to mean "look at" (watch TV, watch a game), so a reader can miss that Paul is listing a physical toll, exhaustion from lack of sleep, right alongside hunger, cold, and fasting.

entries.title: "By and by he is offended" means that eventually, after some time, this person falls away
entries.summary: "By and by" meant immediately, right away, nearly the opposite of its modern sense.
entries.explain:
Matthew 13:21, in the Parable of the Sower, describes the shallow-soil hearer: "when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended." In 1611 English, "by and by" meant "straightway, at once"; this person doesn't gradually drift away over time, they collapse the instant trouble shows up, which is the whole point about shallow roots.

Over the following centuries "by and by" reversed course and came to mean "eventually" or "after a while" (as in the old hymn "we'll understand it better by and by"), so a modern reader gets the timing of the parable exactly backwards.

entries.title: "Then are ye bastards, and not sons" is Scripture using a crude insult or curse word
entries.summary: "Bastard" is used in its strict, literal sense: a child born outside marriage, denied a father's discipline.
entries.explain:
Hebrews 12:8 argues, "if ye be without chastisement, whereof all are partakers, then are ye bastards, and not sons." The logic depends entirely on the literal, legal meaning of the word: in that culture, an illegitimate child typically received no inheritance and little of a father's disciplined attention or training, unlike a legitimate son. So God's discipline of believers is proof they are true sons, not evidence of harshness.

Modern English uses "bastard" almost exclusively as a generic insult or curse word, disconnected from any actual claim about someone's parentage. A reader who only knows that sense hears profanity where the text is making a careful, literal argument about sonship and discipline.

entries.title: "Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast" (1 Chronicles 4:10): modern readers picture Jabez asking for more beachfront, not more territory.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "coast" means border or territory, not a shoreline.
entries.explain:
When Jabez prays "enlarge my coast" in 1 Chronicles 4:10, a modern reader pictures him asking for beachfront property. But Jabez's territory in Judah was interior land, nowhere near the Mediterranean. In the KJV, "coast" regularly translates Hebrew and Greek words for border or territory, not shoreline: you see the same usage in phrases like "the coasts of Judaea" and "the coasts of Tyre and Sidon," all of which are about a boundary line on a map, not a beach.

The word drifted the normal way English words do: "coast" comes from Latin costa, "side" or "edge," and originally meant the edge of anything, a country's edge included. English later narrowed it to mean specifically the edge that meets the sea, leaving the KJV's older, broader sense stranded for modern readers.

entries.title: "All the chief priests and elders of the people took counsel against Jesus to put him to death" (Matthew 27:1): modern readers hear friendly advice-giving, not a death plot.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "counsel" can mean a deliberate scheme or conspiracy, not friendly advice.
entries.explain:
Matthew 27:1 says the chief priests and elders "took counsel against Jesus to put him to death." A modern reader hears "counsel" and pictures a counselor giving advice, or two sides talking something through. Here it means the opposite: this is the KJV's word for hatching a plan or conspiring. The same phrase appears in Psalm 2:2, where "the rulers take counsel together" against God; that's rebellion being organized, not a policy discussion.

"Counsel" in 1611 covered any deliberation toward a decision, good or bad, from godly advice to a death-plot. Modern English kept the friendly-advice half and mostly dropped the conspiratorial half, so today's readers default to the wrong side of the old meaning.

entries.title: "Suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God" (Luke 2:13): modern readers picture a party host, not an army of angels.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "host" means an army or armed multitude, not someone hosting guests.
entries.explain:
Luke 2:13 describes "a multitude of the heavenly host" appearing to the shepherds. Read with modern ears, "host" sounds like the angels are throwing a party. In the KJV it's a military word meaning an army, a body of troops drawn up for battle. That's the same "hosts" in "the LORD of hosts," one of the Bible's most common divine titles, literally "commander of armies."

The word traces to Latin hostis ("army," originally "enemy") by way of Old French. English later split the word in two: the guest-receiving sense of "host" (from a different Latin root, hospes) became the everyday meaning, while the older army sense survived mostly in biblical and liturgical language, which is exactly why it now misleads readers.

entries.title: "He will not have sodden flesh of thee, but raw" (1 Samuel 2:15): modern readers hear "sodden" as soaked or drunk, not boiled.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "sodden" simply means boiled.
entries.explain:
In 1 Samuel 2:15, Eli's corrupt sons' servant demands raw meat instead of "sodden flesh" so the priest can grab the best cuts for roasting before the boiling is even done. A modern reader's ear jumps to "sodden with drink": soaked, saturated, maybe drunk. But in 1611 "sodden" just meant "boiled." It's the old past participle of "seethe" (Old English seoþan, "to boil"): sod was the past tense, sodden the participle, the same pattern as ride/rode/ridden.

Once "boil" took over as the everyday verb, "sodden" drifted into figurative territory: soaked, saturated, and eventually the dull, waterlogged look of a heavy drinker, which is the only sense that survived into modern English. The literal cooking meaning this verse actually uses is gone from everyday speech.

entries.title: "By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD" (Genesis 22:16): modern readers think God swore while alone, not that he swore on his own authority.
entries.summary: "By myself" means "on my own authority," not "unaccompanied."
entries.explain:
After Abraham doesn't withhold Isaac, God tells him, "By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD" (Genesis 22:16). A modern reader hears "by myself" as "alone, with no one else around," as if the point is where God happened to be standing. That's not it. This is an ancient oath formula: you swear by something greater than yourself as a guarantee of the promise. Since nothing outranks God, he swears by his own name and existence instead. Hebrews 6:13 spells this out directly, saying God did this "because he could swear by no greater."

So "by myself" here means something like "on my own authority" or "in my own name"; it's about the source backing the oath, not about solitude.

entries.title: "Avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Timothy 6:20): modern readers think Paul is warning against modern science, not false spiritual knowledge.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "science" just means knowledge in general, not the modern discipline of science.
entries.explain:
Paul warns Timothy to avoid "oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Timothy 6:20). Read today, that sounds like a warning against science itself: biology, physics, and so on. It isn't. The underlying Greek word is gnosis, simply "knowledge," and the KJV translators rendered it "science" because in 1611 that English word just meant "knowledge" broadly, following the Latin scientia. Paul's actual target was a rival system of esoteric religious knowledge, likely an early form of what became Gnosticism, not laboratory work.

English "science" didn't narrow down to mean the systematic study of the natural world until well after the KJV was translated. Plugging in today's meaning turns Paul's warning about false spiritual knowledge into an anti-science proof text it was never meant to be.

entries.title: "And her flowers be upon him, he shall be unclean seven days" (Leviticus 15:24): modern readers picture literal blossoms, not a woman's monthly period.
entries.summary: In the KJV, "flowers" is an old euphemism for a woman's menstrual period.
entries.explain:
Leviticus 15:24 reads, "And if any man lie with her at all, and her flowers be upon him, he shall be unclean seven days." Taken at face value today, "flowers" just sounds like blossoms, which makes the verse baffling. It's actually a delicate, euphemistic KJV term for menstruation: "her flowers" means her monthly flow, and verse 33 uses the identical phrase for "her that is sick of her flowers." Modern translations render it plainly as "menstrual impurity" or "her monthly period."

The usage wasn't unique to the KJV: "flowers" as a polite term for menstruation shows up in English medical and popular writing into the 1600s, echoing the same use of French fleurs. It's simply an old euphemism that dropped out of everyday English, leaving modern readers with only the literal, botanical meaning of the word.

entries.title: "But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me": sounds like Jesus is warning against hurting a child's feelings
entries.summary: In 1611 English, "offend" meant to cause someone to sin or stumble in their faith, not to hurt their feelings.
entries.explain:
In Matthew 18:6, "whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me" translates the Greek skandalizo, the root of our word "scandalize," literally meaning to trip someone into a trap. Jesus isn't warning against insulting a child; he's warning against leading a believer into sin, doubt, or spiritual ruin.

The word appears this way throughout the Gospels (Matthew 5:29-30, 11:6, 13:41), always carrying the sense of "cause to stumble" rather than "upset." The modern, narrower meaning (wounded feelings) is a much later development that had already begun by the 19th century but wasn't the KJV translators' meaning in 1611.
entries.tags: offend kjv archaic skandalizo stumble sin

entries.title: "Ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars": reads like Jesus is warning specifically about false gossip and misinformation spreading before the end times
entries.summary: In the KJV, "rumour" simply meant a report or piece of news, true or false, not gossip presumed to be false.
entries.explain:
Matthew 24:6 reads, "And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars: see that ye be not troubled." The word comes from Latin rumor, meaning "noise, common talk, a current report with or without foundation." It described news traveling by word of mouth, accurate or not, not the modern sense of a story assumed to be unverified or false.

Jesus is saying disciples will hear both of actual wars nearby and reports of wars happening elsewhere, and neither should shake them. He isn't singling out misinformation as a distinct sign; "rumour" here is just "news you've heard secondhand."
entries.tags: rumour rumor kjv archaic report news

entries.title: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus": sounds like a promise that believers will never be criticized or disapproved of
entries.summary: "Condemnation" in the KJV is courtroom language: a legal guilty verdict and sentence, not moral disapproval or criticism.
entries.explain:
Romans 8:1 says "there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus." The underlying Greek word means a judicial sentence or penalty. Paul isn't promising believers will never be disapproved of or made to feel bad; he's saying they will never face the legal verdict of "guilty" before God's tribunal.

The same courtroom sense runs through John 3:17, where God did not send his Son "to condemn the world," meaning to pass judicial sentence on it, but to save it. Modern English has flattened "condemn" into a word for expressing strong disapproval ("I condemn that behavior"), which loses the specifically legal, sentence-passing weight it carried for the KJV translators.
entries.tags: condemn condemnation kjv archaic legal judicial verdict

entries.title: "And he entreated Abram well for her sake": sounds like Pharaoh was begging or pleading with Abram
entries.summary: In the KJV, "entreated" often just meant "treated" or "dealt with," not "begged" or "pleaded with."
entries.explain:
Genesis 12:16 says of Pharaoh, "he entreated Abram well for her sake": meaning Pharaoh treated Abram favorably and gave him generous gifts because of Sarai, not that Pharaoh begged Abram for anything. "Entreat" in this sense is simply an older form of "treat," used with an adverb of manner ("entreated well," "evil entreated," "spitefully entreated") to describe how one person handled another.

This is a different use from the more familiar KJV "intreat," which does mean "beg" or "implore" (as in Ruth's "intreat me not to leave thee"). The two spellings were used somewhat interchangeably by the translators, which is exactly why the "treat/deal with" sense of "entreat" gets missed by modern readers who only know the "beg" meaning.
entries.tags: entreat intreat kjv archaic treat deal

entries.title: "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth": sounds like Christians should chase after other people's money or riches for them
entries.summary: "Wealth" in the KJV meant general well-being or welfare, not money or material riches.
entries.explain:
1 Corinthians 10:24 reads, "Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth." The word "wealth" is related to "weal" (as in "commonweal" or "public weal") and in 1611 meant "welfare" or "good" broadly: moral, spiritual, and physical flourishing, not financial prosperity. The underlying Greek is simply a word for "good" or "advantage," with no reference to money at all. The setting makes the point for itself: Paul is in the middle of an argument about food and conscience, not about money. The Old English behind the word is wela, well-being.

Paul's point is that Christians should prioritize what's genuinely good for other people rather than their own preferences, not that they should go make other people rich. English narrowed "wealth" down to mean money specifically well after 1611, leaving modern readers with the wrong picture entirely.
entries.tags: wealth kjv archaic welfare wellbeing good

entries.title: "Whither have ye made a road to day?": sounds like David was asked which highway or street he'd built
entries.summary: In the KJV, a "road" was a military raid or incursion, not a paved route for travel.
entries.explain:
In 1 Samuel 27:10, the Philistine king Achish asks David, "Whither have ye made a road to day?" and David answers with the territory he'd attacked: "against the south of Judah... the Jerahmeelites... the Kenites." Modern translations render this plainly as "raid." "Road" comes from the same root as "ride" and originally meant a mounted expedition or foray, especially a hostile one, before it settled into meaning the path itself.

A reader today pictures asphalt and construction; the actual exchange is a warlord casually asking a mercenary captain who he'd just plundered.
entries.tags: road kjv archaic raid incursion military

entries.title: "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children": sounds like a call to simply trail behind God or be one of his fans
entries.summary: "Followers" in the KJV translates the Greek for "imitators": actively copying God's character, not just tagging along.
entries.explain:
Ephesians 5:1 says, "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children." The Greek word is mimetai, the root of our word "mimic," meaning someone who actively copies or reproduces another's pattern of life, not a passive follower or fan trailing behind. Paul uses the same word elsewhere to tell believers to imitate Christ and imitate faithful church leaders.

The modern sense of "follower" (someone who trails after, watches, or subscribes to another, as in "social media followers") is far more passive than what the verse asks for: consciously modeling your own conduct (kindness, forgiveness, love) on God's, the way a child mimics a parent.

entries.title: "All the world should be taxed" (Luke 2:1): sounds like Caesar rolled out an income tax
entries.summary: "Taxed" in 1611 English meant enrolled for a census, not billed for money.
entries.explain:
Luke 2:1 reads, "there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed," and verse 3 adds "all went to be taxed, every one into his own city." A modern reader pictures Rome sending out tax bills. But the Greek word behind it (apographo) means "to register" or "enroll," and that's exactly why Joseph and Mary had to travel to Bethlehem: this was a headcount for the empire's records, not a bill in the mail.

Modern translations (ESV, NIV, NASB) render it "a census be taken" or "registered" for exactly this reason. Actual Roman taxation could follow such a registration, but the word "taxed" itself is doing 1611 duty for "counted and listed," not "charged money."

entries.title: "Used curious arts" (Acts 19:19): sounds like Ephesians were just intellectually curious
entries.summary: "Curious arts" in 1611 English meant occult practices and sorcery, not idle curiosity.
entries.explain:
Acts 19:19 says, "Many of them also which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men: and they counted the price of them, and found it fifty thousand pieces of silver." A modern reader hears "curious" and pictures people who just liked to ask questions. But Ephesus was famous in the ancient world for magical texts and spells (the so-called "Ephesian writings"), and "curious" here carries its older sense of "skillfully or elaborately made/wrought" applied to occult craft: this is a mass book-burning of sorcery manuals, not a library clearance.

Modern translations make it explicit: the NIV and CSB both render the phrase "practiced sorcery" or "magic arts." The fifty thousand pieces of silver (roughly 150 years of a laborer's wages) signals just how serious and widespread this magical trade was before these new converts torched it.

entries.title: "It shall bruise thy head" (Genesis 3:15): sounds like a minor skin bruise, like bumping your head
entries.summary: "Bruise" in Genesis 3:15 translates a Hebrew verb far stronger than the modern word, usually given as crush or strike at.
entries.explain:
Genesis 3:15 reads, "it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel." A modern reader thinks of a bruise as a sore purple mark that heals in a week, hardly a fitting punishment for the serpent or a fitting wound for the woman's offspring. The underlying Hebrew word, shuph, is rare in the Old Testament, and its range of meaning runs to "strike," "crush," or "trample underfoot," not a mild contusion.

This is why the verse is often called the "protoevangelium" (first gospel): it pictures a decisive, head-crushing blow against the serpent, even while the serpent only manages to strike the heel. "Bruise" was a serviceable 1611 word for a heavy blow, but English has since narrowed it down to something much lighter, and that shift blunts the force of the promise.

entries.title: "Now I beseech you, brethren" (1 Corinthians 1:10): sounds like Paul is addressing only the men in the church
entries.summary: "Brethren" translates a Greek word that regularly addressed whole congregations, women included, not just the men.
entries.explain:
1 Corinthians 1:10 opens, "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing." To modern English ears, "brethren" sounds like it's speaking to the male members only, since "brother" today means a male sibling, full stop. But the underlying Greek word, adelphoi, functioned in first-century usage as the standard plural for a mixed group, and Paul plainly has the whole church in view here, since he goes on discussing women praying and prophesying just two chapters later (1 Corinthians 11).

This is exactly why modern translations like the NIV and CSB now render adelphoi as "brothers and sisters" in these congregational addresses. The KJV isn't wrong so much as dated: "brethren" was a fine stand-in for a gender-inclusive term in 1611, but English "brethren" has since drifted to sound exclusively male, misleading readers about who Paul was actually talking to.

entries.title: "The valley of the passengers" (Ezekiel 39:11): sounds like a highway rest stop for bus and plane passengers
entries.summary: "Passengers" in 1611 English just meant people passing through on foot, not riders in a vehicle.
entries.explain:
Ezekiel 39:11 says God will give Gog "a place there of graves in Israel, the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea: and it shall stop the noses of the passengers." A modern reader hears "passengers" and thinks of people riding in a car, bus, or plane. But the word translates the Hebrew 'oberim, "those who pass through or over": ordinary travelers on foot or by caravan, walking the route through that valley.

The valley gets renamed "Hamon-Gog" (multitude of Gog) after it becomes a mass burial ground so vast that it blocks the road and literally "stops the nose" of anyone passing by, because of the stench. "Passengers" here is just an older, more literal use of the word (people in the act of passing by) centuries before it narrowed to mean someone riding along in a vehicle.

entries.title: "She constantly affirmed that it was even so" (Acts 12:15): sounds like Rhoda kept saying it nonstop for hours
entries.summary: "Constantly" in 1611 English meant firmly and insistently, not "nonstop over time."
entries.explain:
In Acts 12:15, after the servant girl Rhoda recognizes Peter's voice at the gate and the praying believers tell her she's out of her mind, the text says, "But she constantly affirmed that it was even so." A modern reader pictures Rhoda repeating herself over and over for an extended stretch of time, since today "constantly" means "continuously, without stopping." But the 1611 sense of "constant" is closer to its Latin root constans ("standing firm"), meaning she held her ground and insisted with unwavering certainty, not that she literally kept talking nonstop.

Modern translations bring this out as "she kept insisting that it was so" (ESV, NIV), which captures firm conviction under pushback rather than a marathon of repetition. The same shift shows up in Titus 3:8, where believers are told to be careful to "affirm constantly" good works, again firmly and resolutely, not endlessly.

entries.title: "Certain lewd fellows of the baser sort" (Acts 17:5): sounds like a gang of sexually indecent men
entries.summary: "Lewd" in 1611 English meant base, worthless, or wicked in general, not sexually indecent as it does today.
entries.explain:
Acts 17:5 describes jealous opponents in Thessalonica who "took unto them certain lewd fellows of the baser sort, and gathered a company, and set all the city on an uproar." A modern reader assumes "lewd" is about sexual misconduct, since that's the word's entire meaning now. But in 1611 English, "lewd" traced back to a word for the unlearned or common laity, and by Shakespeare's day it had broadened into a general put-down for anyone worthless, base, or morally low, with no sexual content required.

That's why modern translations render the phrase "wicked men from the marketplace" (CSB) or "some bad characters from the marketplace" (NIV), essentially rent-a-mob loiterers hired to stir up a riot, not a specific charge of sexual sin. The word's meaning has since narrowed hard toward sex, so the KJV phrase reads very differently today than it did to its original audience.

entries.title: even him did outlandish women cause to sin: sounds like Solomon was led astray by bizarre, wildly weird women
entries.summary: In 1611, "outlandish" just meant "from another land" (foreign), not bizarre or weird.
entries.explain:
Nehemiah 13:26 says Solomon sinned because "even him did outlandish women cause to sin." Read with today's ears, that sounds like the women were strange or eccentric. But "outlandish" is literally out-land-ish: belonging to an outside land, i.e., foreign. Nehemiah is talking about Solomon's non-Israelite wives who pulled him into idol worship (1 Kings 11), not women with odd behavior.

The drift makes sense: something "of another land" eventually became "weird by our standards," and by the 20th century "outlandish" had fully shifted to mean bizarre or outrageous, its original geographic sense gone.

entries.title: instructing those that oppose themselves: sounds like people working against their own interests, self-sabotaging
entries.summary: "Oppose themselves" in 1611 English meant "set themselves in opposition" (they're opponents), not that they're contradicting or sabotaging themselves.
entries.explain: 2 Timothy 2:25 tells Timothy to be gentle "in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves." A modern reader hears "oppose themselves" as reflexive in the self-defeating sense: people who fight their own interests. But the underlying Greek word is a middle-voice verb that simply means "to be adverse, to be an opponent." The KJV's "themselves" is just carrying over that Greek middle-voice grammar into English; it isn't claiming these people are self-contradictory. Paul is talking about opponents of the truth whom Timothy is to correct with patience, not people undermining themselves.

entries.title: let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her: reads like grain that somehow belongs to "purpose," or grain with a mission
entries.summary: "Of purpose" was just 1611 phrasing for "on purpose": deliberately.
entries.explain: In Ruth 2:16, Boaz orders his young men: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." Modern English pairs "purpose" with "on," not "of," so the phrase can trip a reader into parsing it oddly. But "of purpose" was simply the standard 1611 way of saying "deliberately" or "intentionally." Boaz is quietly instructing his workers to drop extra grain on purpose so Ruth can glean more than she'd normally be entitled to: a deliberate act of provision dressed up as an accident.

entries.title: strong drink is raging: sounds like alcohol makes people simply feel angry
entries.summary: In 1611, "raging" described violent, riotous, out-of-control behavior in general, not just the emotion of anger.
entries.explain: Proverbs 20:1 reads, "Wine is a mocker, strong drink is raging: and whosoever is deceived thereby is not wise." A modern reader narrows "raging" down to hot anger. The word's older range was broader: tumultuous, violent, unruly conduct (brawling, carrying on, being out of control), which is exactly why modern translations render the same line as "strong drink is a brawler" (NIV, ESV). The proverb isn't just warning that drink makes you mad; it's warning that it turns you riotous and reckless generally.

entries.title: the people imagine a vain thing: sounds like people are just picturing something silly in their heads
entries.summary: In 1611, "imagine" meant to plot or scheme, not to picture something mentally.
entries.explain: Psalm 2:1 asks, "Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?" Today "imagine" is a mild, even playful word: picturing something in your mind. But the underlying Hebrew (hagah) means to mutter, plan, or devise: the same root rendered "meditate" one psalm earlier in Psalm 1:2. The nations aren't daydreaming; they're actively scheming and plotting rebellion against God and his anointed king, and the psalm calls that plot futile ("a vain thing"). "Imagine" here is a synonym for "conspire," not "fantasize."

entries.title: desire the sincere milk of the word: sounds like the word of God is being described as honest or heartfelt
entries.summary: In 1611, "sincere" meant pure and unadulterated, not "honest" or "heartfelt."
entries.explain:
1 Peter 2:2 urges believers, "as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby." Today "sincere" describes a person's genuine feelings or honesty. In 1611 it described a substance: unmixed, unadulterated, without any foreign additive: which is why modern translations render this verse "pure spiritual milk." Peter's image is infant formula with nothing false stirred into it, not a claim that Scripture is emotionally genuine.

One popular story claims "sincere" comes from Latin sine cera, "without wax": supposedly because honest merchants marked pottery that wasn't patched with wax to hide cracks. It's a great story, but it's a folk etymology: reputable references including the Oxford English Dictionary and etymonline reject it, tracing "sincere" instead to Latin sincerus, "whole, unmixed, genuine." The real meaning holds up even though the wax story doesn't.

entries.title: preach the gospel to every creature: sounds like a command to evangelize animals
entries.summary: In 1611, "creature" meant anything created: here it means every human being, not an animal.
entries.explain: In the Great Commission of Mark 16:15, Jesus says, "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Modern English has narrowed "creature" down to animals, or worse, monsters. But the word simply comes from "created thing": anything God made. In this command it refers to every human being on earth, not beasts of the field. The same broad, "everything God made" sense shows up in Romans 8:19-22, where Paul says "the creature was made subject to vanity" and will one day be "delivered from the bondage of corruption": meaning creation itself, not a cast of animals.

entries.title: Colossians 2:23's "will worship" refers to worship offered willingly, out of eager devotion.
entries.summary: In 1611 English "will worship" meant religion you invent for yourself, not worship done with a willing heart.
entries.explain:
Colossians 2:23 (KJV) reads: "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body: not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh." The phrase translates the Greek ethelothrēskia, a compound coined from "self-chosen" plus "worship": religious rules a person makes up and imposes on themselves rather than ones God actually commanded. It's a rebuke, not a compliment.

The trap is that modern English defaults to reading "will" as intent or enthusiasm: "I'll do this gladly." But 1611 "will worship" used "will" in the older sense of self-willed or arbitrary: worship of your own devising. Paul isn't praising eager worshippers here; he's warning against man-made asceticism dressed up as spirituality.

entries.title: Genesis 1:28's command to "replenish the earth" tells Adam and Eve to refill or restock a planet that had already been populated once and emptied out.
entries.summary: In 1611 English "replenish" simply meant "fill up": it carried no built-in idea of refilling something previously emptied.
entries.explain:
Genesis 1:28 (KJV) reads: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it." The Hebrew verb behind it, male' (מָלֵא), just means "fill": the same word used for filling a cup or a room, with no notion of "again." When the KJV translators chose "replenish" (from Old French replenir, from Latin replere), it was simply the era's word for "fill completely"; it hadn't yet picked up the modern sense of restocking something used up.

This case gets cited in young-earth arguments claiming "re-plenish" proves a prior population wiped out before Genesis 1. That reading leans on a sense "replenish" acquired later in English, not the sense it carried in 1611 or the sense of the Hebrew word it translates. Both point to "fill," not "refill." That's a real, contested case rather than one This record settles theologically.

entries.title: In 1 Samuel 14:8, Jonathan says he and his armor-bearer will "discover" themselves to the Philistines: meaning they'll find out something new about them.
entries.summary: In 1611 English "discover" meant "uncover" or "expose": Jonathan is planning to reveal himself, not learn something unknown.
entries.explain:
1 Samuel 14:8 (KJV) reads: "Then said Jonathan, Behold, we will pass over unto these men, and we will discover ourselves unto them." Jonathan isn't proposing an investigation: he means "we'll step into the open where they can see us." The underlying Hebrew galah means "to uncover, expose, lay bare," and 1611 "discover" tracked that meaning directly: built from "dis-" (undo) plus "cover," to discover something was to strip away its covering.

Proverbs 25:9 uses the word the same old way: "discover not a secret to another" means don't reveal it, not don't find it out. The now-dominant sense, "find something previously unknown," grew out of this older meaning but hadn't taken over by 1611.

entries.title: Romans 1:29 lists "debate" alongside murder and envy, as if the Bible is condemning formal argument or reasoned disagreement.
entries.summary: In 1611 English "debate" meant strife and quarreling, not a civil, structured argument.
entries.explain:
Romans 1:29 (KJV) reads: "Being filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity." The Greek word translated "debate" is eris, the same word Galatians 5:20 renders "strife," describing destructive rivalry and contentious wrangling driven by pride, not a search for truth.

Modern "debate" suggests something respectable: a classroom or parliamentary debate. But 1611 "debate" carried the older, more hostile sense of quarreling and contention. Paul isn't condemning reasoned disagreement here; he's condemning strife-mongering, closer to what we'd now call feuding.

entries.title: Acts 17:23 says Paul noticed the Athenians' "devotions": meaning he observed them in personal prayer or a quiet time.
entries.summary: In 1611 English "devotions" meant the physical objects of worship (idols, altars, shrines), not private prayer time.
entries.explain:
Acts 17:23 (KJV) reads: "For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD."
